abstract: "Psychologists increasingly report the probability of direction ($pd$), the posterior probability that a parameter lies on the side of the null value favored by the posterior, and claim a direction when $pd$ reaches a fixed threshold such as .975. Applied to many parameters, this rule produces more wrong claims as tests accumulate. We present an adjustment based on the classical Bayesian response to multiplicity, a penalty on the prior odds of each claim. The claimed direction is known only after the data, so the penalty must cover both directions. The researcher thus sets in advance $\\bar{\\pi}$, an upper bound on the prior probability of each direction, the same for every parameter in the family. A claim is made only if its posterior probability still reaches the threshold when its direction receives prior probability $1 - \\bar{\\pi}$. The adjustment uses only the $pd$ values and holds whenever the priors used to fit the model are continuous and symmetric about the null value. Because a directional claim about a null effect is false, the proportion of effects in the family that could be null offers a reference value for $\\bar{\\pi}$. Simulations with independent and correlated parameters show how the false discovery rate, the family-wise error rate, and power depend on $\\bar{\\pi}$, set below, at, or above the proportion of null effects. We also compare the rule with two alternative procedures, joint directional statements and simultaneous credible intervals. All three are implemented in the accompanying R package *multibayes*."

Over the past two decades, the use of Bayesian methods in psychological research has grown considerably [@Van2017; @Jevremov2024; @Pfadt2025]. This expansion has, however, been accompanied by practices reminiscent of the "null ritual" in frequentist statistics, where widespread adoption gave way to automatic application rather than principled reasoning [@Gigerenzer2004; @Cohen1994]. Researchers sometimes treat Bayes factor thresholds (e.g., BF > 3) as dichotomous decision rules, or claim that an effect "exists" because the posterior probability of a directional effect exceeds a conventional benchmark such as .975 [@Heck2023; @Kelter2023; @Tendeiro2024; @Hoijtink2016; @Tendeiro2019; @Kruschke2018]. Such cutoffs are convenient, but they encourage all-or-none interpretations. Moreover, when the same cutoff is applied to parameter after parameter, the resulting decisions face the multiplicity problem long recognized in frequentist statistics.

Frequentists developed methods to address this problem, controlling either the Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER; the probability of at least one false positive) or the False Discovery Rate (FDR; the expected proportion of false positives among rejected hypotheses) [@Benjamini1995; @Westfall1993]. These procedures address whether a spurious result enters the literature, but leave unresolved a subtler consequence of the same selection process. When researchers examine many parameters but highlight only the most extreme estimates, selection systematically inflates reported magnitudes [@Gelman2014; @Zwet2021; @Altoe2020]. Bayesian methods can mitigate this overestimation, pulling extreme estimates toward more plausible values through informative priors [@Zwet2022; @Dawid1994] and hierarchical modeling [@Gelman2012; @GelmanBook; @Kruschke2011; @Berry1999]. Magnitude bias and false-positive accumulation are, however, distinct problems. Shrinkage offers no guarantee about the error properties of a decision rule applied across many parameters: if the same cutoff is used repeatedly (e.g., claiming an effect whenever a posterior probability exceeds .975), the probability of spurious findings can remain substantial. Bayesian responses to this issue do exist, such as joint probability statements [@Gelman2000; @Pruzek2016; @Schnell2020; @Box1992] or priors over the hypothesis space that scale with the number of tests [@Scott2006; @Scott2010; @Jeffreys1938; @Westfall1997].

Here we focus on a decision rule based on the probability of direction ($pd$), which is increasingly used in psychological research [@Stone2024; @Brissenden2023; @Hochman2025; @Makowski2020; @Brissenden2024; @Ciranka2026; @Schurr2024; @Ben2022; @Bramley2022]. The $pd$ is the posterior probability that a parameter lies in its dominant direction [@Makowski2019; @Shi2021], and a direction is claimed when $pd$ exceeds a fixed threshold (e.g., $.95$ or $.975$). We examine the frequentist operating characteristics^[Although frequentist and Bayesian frameworks rest on different foundations, examining the frequentist operating characteristics of a Bayesian procedure (how it behaves over repeated use) is a well-established practice [@Zhang2019; @Ventz2015; @Müller2004].] of this rule and address the resulting multiplicity problem with the second strategy noted above, a penalty on the prior odds of each claim. This penalty is the classical Bayesian response to multiplicity, introduced by @Jeffreys1938 and developed by @Westfall1997, and it underlies more recent Bayesian approaches to FDR control [@Scott2006; @Scott2010; @Guo2010; @Abraham2022; @Efron2001; @Storey2003; @Storey2002] as well as the post hoc correction implemented in JASP [@Bergh2020; @deJong2019].

To our knowledge, the penalty has not been applied to $pd$. The obstacle is that the direction of a claim based on $pd$ is chosen by the data, so the penalty cannot be attached to a direction fixed in advance. Following robust Bayesian analysis [@Berger1994], we therefore lower the prior odds of both directions. Before the data, the researcher sets $\bar{\pi}$, an upper bound on the prior probability of each direction of a parameter, and uses the same value for every parameter in the family. We then consider the set of priors that give each direction a prior probability between $1 - \bar{\pi}$ and $\bar{\pi}$, and accept a claim only if it holds under all of them, that is, if its posterior probability still reaches the usual threshold when its direction receives prior probability $1 - \bar{\pi}$. The value of $\bar{\pi}$ thus expresses how skeptical the researcher is of a directional claim. Because a directional claim about a null effect is false, the proportion of effects in the family that could be null offers a reference value for $\bar{\pi}$.

The paper proceeds as follows. We first introduce $pd$ and the rule based on it, and show why the rule produces more false directional claims as the number of tests grows. We then derive the adjustment, which needs only the $pd$ values, and discuss how to choose $\bar{\pi}$. A simulation study with independent and correlated parameters then shows how the FDR, the FWER, and power depend on $\bar{\pi}$, including values below and above the actual proportion of null effects, and compares the rule with joint directional statements and simultaneous credible intervals. Finally, we illustrate with a worked example the R package `multibayes`, which implements all three procedures, and conclude with a general discussion.

# Probability of Direction

The probability of direction ($pd$) is a posterior summary that quantifies how strongly the posterior distribution favors one direction of a parameter $\theta$ relative to a reference value $\theta_{\text{null}}$ [@Makowski2019]. For a continuous posterior, it can be defined as the larger of the two one-sided posterior probabilities, $pd = \max(\Pr(\theta < \theta_{\text{null}} \mid y),\ \Pr(\theta > \theta_{\text{null}} \mid y))$, and it ranges from .5 (no directional preference) to 1 (all on one side). The $pd$ equals exactly the complement of the one-sided $p$-value when computed on the posterior of a location parameter in exponential-family models estimated under a uniform prior; under a broader class of priors, this correspondence holds approximately [@Marsman2017; @Casella1987; @Shi2021]. For ease of exposition, we set $\theta_{\text{null}} = 0$ throughout; it can take any other value, which is particularly relevant when hypotheses involve a minimum effect of practical interest.

In practice, $pd$ is often used to summarize both the direction and the existence of an effect. This use is clearest when phrased as a decision rule, $pd \geq c$, which requires the posterior to assign at least $c$ probability mass to the side of $0$ it favors. Setting $c = 1 - \alpha/2$ is convenient because it bounds the posterior mass on the other side of $0$ by $\alpha/2$. For concreteness, suppose the posterior favors positive values, so that $pd = \Pr(\theta > 0 \mid y)$. With $\alpha = .05$, $c = .975$, and the rule requires $\Pr(\theta \le 0 \mid y) \leq .025$. The rule $pd \geq .975$ is therefore the same as the common practice of claiming an effect when the central 95% equal-tailed credible interval does not extend past $0$ (@fig-pd-ci), which is often read as showing that $0$ is relatively implausible [@Box1992]. Like the reference value of $0$, the threshold $c = .975$ is chosen only for ease of exposition, and any other posterior probability cutoff can be used.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pd-ci
#| fig-cap: "The Probability of Direction and the 95% Credible Interval"
#| apa-note: >
#|   Two normal posteriors for a parameter $\theta$, with the posterior mass below $0$ in orange and above $0$ in blue; the black bar is the central 95% equal-tailed credible interval. Panel A: $pd \geq .975$, and the interval does not extend past $0$. Panel B: $pd < .975$, and the interval includes $0$.
#| fig-width: 10.2
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# one panel: normal posterior with mean mu and sd s, shaded by side of 0
pd_ci_plot <- function(mu, s, tag) {
  x  <- seq(-1, 1, length.out = 2001)
  d  <- data.frame(x = x, y = dnorm(x, mu, s), side = ifelse(x > 0, "pos", "neg"))
  ci <- qnorm(c(0.025, 0.975), mu, s)
  p_pos <- 1 - pnorm(0, mu, s)
  # plotmath labels, one per line, so theta is drawn as a symbol
  lab <- c(sprintf('Pr(theta > 0 ~ "|" ~ italic(y)) == "%s"', nz(p_pos, 3)),
           sprintf('Pr(theta < 0 ~ "|" ~ italic(y)) == "%s"', nz(1 - p_pos, 3)),
           sprintf('italic(pd) == "%s"', nz(max(p_pos, 1 - p_pos), 3)),
           sprintf('"95%% CI = [%.2f, %.2f]"', ci[1], ci[2]))
  ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_area(aes(fill = side), show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey40") +
    annotate("segment", x = ci[1], xend = ci[2], y = 0, yend = 0, linewidth = 2.5, lineend = "round") +
    annotate("rect", xmin = -1, xmax = -0.1, ymin = 1.2, ymax = 2.45, fill = "white", colour = "grey30") +
    annotate("text", x = -0.96, y = c(2.25, 1.95, 1.65, 1.35), label = lab, parse = TRUE, hjust = 0, size = 4.2) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(neg = "#F8A31B", pos = "deepskyblue3")) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-0.5, 0, 0.5, 1)) +
    labs(x = expression(theta), y = "Posterior density", title = tag) +
    theme_clean(14) + theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
}
pd_ci_plot(0.35, 0.16, "A") | pd_ci_plot(0.30, 0.16, "B")
```

How often the rule $pd \geq c$ claims a direction when $\theta = 0$ depends on how $pd$ varies across repeated samples, and hence on the model and the prior. All illustrations and simulations use the normal model, as a representative case of parameters whose posterior is approximately normal. For a parameter $\theta$, $n$ independent observations are drawn from $\mathcal{N}(\theta, 1)$, and $\theta$ has the prior $\mathcal{N}(0, \tau)$, where $\tau$ is the prior standard deviation, so that the posterior of $\theta$ is also normal. Small values of $\tau$ give a narrow prior, concentrated near $0$, and large values a diffuse one. 

In this model, for a null effect ($\theta = 0$) under a diffuse prior, $pd$ is approximately uniform on $[.5, 1]$ across repeated samples (@fig-uniform-pd, $\tau = 2$). The rule $pd \geq c$ with $c = 1 - \alpha/2$ therefore claims a direction with probability about $\alpha$. A narrow prior shrinks $pd$ toward $.5$ and lowers this probability (@fig-uniform-pd, $\tau = 0.2$), but only for each test separately. With any fixed prior, the probability that at least one of $pd_1, \dots, pd_m$ reaches $c$ still grows with the number of tests $m$. For $m = 10$ independent tests of null effects with $n = 50$, for example, it is about $`r nz(fwer_null(10, 50, 2), 2)`$ under the diffuse prior and $`r nz(fwer_null(10, 50, 0.2), 2)`$ under the narrow one.


```{r}
#| label: fig-uniform-pd
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of the Probability of Direction Under the Null"
#| apa-note: >
#|   Density of $pd$ across repeated samples when $\theta = 0$, for observations $y_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta, 1)$ and a normal prior $\theta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau)$, by sample size $n$ (rows) and prior standard deviation $\tau$ (columns). With a diffuse prior ($\tau = 2$), $pd$ is approximately uniform on $[.5, 1]$; a narrow prior ($\tau = 0.2$) shrinks it toward $.5$, especially in small samples. Bin width = 0.025.
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 9
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Distribution function of pd under the null in the conjugate normal-normal model
pd_cdf <- function(p, n, tau) {
  s <- sqrt((n * tau^2) / (1 + n * tau^2))
  2 * pnorm(qnorm(p) / s) - 1
}
bin_width <- 0.025
breaks_pd <- seq(0.5, 1, by = bin_width)
grid_pd <- expand.grid(lower = breaks_pd[-length(breaks_pd)],
                       n = c(30, 50, 100), tau = c(0.2, 0.5, 2)) |>
  mutate(upper   = lower + bin_width,
         mid     = lower + bin_width / 2,
         density = (pd_cdf(upper, n, tau) - pd_cdf(lower, n, tau)) / bin_width,
         n_lab   = factor(sprintf("italic(n) == %d", n),
                          levels = sprintf("italic(n) == %d", c(30, 50, 100))),
         tau_lab = factor(sprintf("tau == %s", tau),
                          levels = sprintf("tau == %s", c(0.2, 0.5, 2))))

ggplot(grid_pd, aes(x = mid, y = density)) +
  geom_col(width = bin_width * 0.9, fill = "#F5A623", color = NA) +
  facet_grid(n_lab ~ tau_lab, labeller = label_parsed) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0.5, 1, by = 0.1)) +
  labs(x = expression(italic(pd)), y = "Density") +
  theme_clean(base_size = 14)
```

# Penalizing the Prior Odds of a Directional Claim

To limit the false claims that accumulate across tests, we penalize the prior odds of each directional claim, following @Jeffreys1938 and @Westfall1997.

## From the Probability of Direction to the Bayes Factor

As in the previous section, suppose that the posterior favors positive values. The claim is then that $\theta > 0$, which we denote $H_{+}$, and the opposite direction, $\theta < 0$, we denote $H_{-}$. We call the prior on $\theta$ specified in the fitted model the *estimation prior*, because the parameters are estimated under it. We assume that it is continuous and symmetric about $0$, as are normal or Student-$t$ priors centered on $0$ and, as a limit, flat priors. Symmetry makes $H_{+}$ and  $H_{-}$ equally probable a priori, $\Pr(H_{+}) = \Pr(H_{-}) = .5$, and after the data $pd = \Pr(H_{+} \mid y)$ and $1 - pd = \Pr(H_{-} \mid y)$.

The ratio $pd/(1 - pd)$ is therefore the posterior odds of $H_{+}$ against $H_{-}$, that is, how many times more probable $H_{+}$ is than $H_{-}$ after the data. By Bayes' rule, the posterior odds are the product of two terms,
$$
\frac{\Pr(H_{+} \mid y)}{\Pr(H_{-} \mid y)} = \text{BF}_{+-} \times \frac{\Pr(H_{+})}{\Pr(H_{-})}.
$$
The second term, the prior odds, says how many times more probable $H_{+}$ is than $H_{-}$ before the data. The first, the Bayes factor $\text{BF}_{+-}$, says by how much the data change these odds. Under the symmetric estimation prior, the prior odds are $.5/.5 = 1$, so the posterior odds equal the Bayes factor [@Marsman2017],
$$
\frac{pd}{1 - pd} = \text{BF}_{+-}.
$$
For a parameter with $pd = .988$, for example, $\text{BF}_{+-} = .988/.012 \approx 82$, so the data are about 82 times more probable under $H_{+}$ than under $H_{-}$.

The rule $pd \geq c$ can thus be written as a rule on the Bayes factor. Because the odds $pd/(1 - pd)$ increase with $pd$,
$$
pd \geq c \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \frac{pd}{1 - pd} \geq \frac{c}{1 - c} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \text{BF}_{+-} \geq \frac{c}{1 - c}.
$$
With $c = .975$, a direction is claimed whenever the Bayes factor is at least $.975/.025 = 39$. Because the prior odds are fixed at one, the Bayes factor alone decides every claim.

## Prior Odds With Many Tests

Consider now a family of $m$ tests, indexed by $i = 1, \dots, m$, each concerning a parameter $\theta_i$ with probability of direction $pd_i$. Under the symmetric estimation prior, each parameter is equally likely to be positive or negative before the data. Whichever direction is later claimed, the claim is therefore false with prior probability $.5$. If the parameters are independent a priori, the prior probability that all $m$ claims are false, an event we denote $H_0$, is the product of these probabilities, $.5^m$. With $m = 5$, $\Pr(H_0) = .5^{5} \approx .03$, so before any data the estimation prior gives probability $1 - .03 = .97$ to at least one claim in the family being correct. This probability approaches one as more parameters are tested, which may not represent the researcher's beliefs. The rule $pd \geq c$, however, keeps the prior odds of every claim at one, as if each parameter were the only one tested.

The classical response is to lower the prior odds of each claim, so that the prior of each parameter also expresses what the researcher believes about the family as a whole, for example that all the claims could be false with a probability much larger than $.5^m$. To see how the prior odds are lowered, suppose first that the direction of a parameter is predicted before the data, say $\theta > 0$. The researcher then gives the opposite direction, $H_{-}$, a prior probability $\pi$ larger than $.5$, and $H_{+}$ the probability $1 - \pi$, so the prior odds of $H_{+}$ become $(1 - \pi)/\pi$, below one.

The prior odds can be lowered without changing the shape of the estimation prior on either side of $0$. For the prior $\mathcal{N}(0, \tau)$ of the normal model, let $\mathcal{N}_{-}(0, \tau)$ and $\mathcal{N}_{+}(0, \tau)$ denote this normal truncated to negative and to positive values, so that the estimation prior is $.5\,\mathcal{N}_{-} + .5\,\mathcal{N}_{+}$. The reweighted prior
$$
\pi\,\mathcal{N}_{-}(0, \tau) + (1 - \pi)\,\mathcal{N}_{+}(0, \tau)
$$
moves probability from the positive to the negative side and keeps the shape within each side. The likelihood averaged over each side, and hence the Bayes factor $pd/(1 - pd)$, is the same as under the estimation prior. Only the prior odds change, and the posterior odds of $H_{+}$ become 
$$\text{BF}_{+-} \times \frac{1 - \pi}{\pi}.$$

The remaining question is how large $\pi$ should be. @Jeffreys1938 and @Westfall1997 fixed the prior probability of $H_0$ in advance, at the same value whatever the size of the family. With the penalty, $\Pr(H_0) = \pi^m$ for independent parameters, so keeping $\Pr(H_0)$ fixed requires $\pi$ to grow with $m$. Fixing $\Pr(H_0) = .5$, for example, makes the event that all claims are false and the event that at least one claim is correct equally probable before the data, and gives $\pi = .5^{1/m}$, which is $`r nz(.5^(1/2), 2)`$ for $m = 2$, $`r nz(.5^(1/5), 2)`$ for $m = 5$, and $`r nz(.5^(1/20), 2)`$ for $m = 20$. A larger $\pi$ gives smaller prior odds, so the Bayes factor needed for a claim grows with $m$, much as the per-test threshold does in the frequentist Bonferroni correction [@Westfall1997].


## A Set of Priors Penalizing Either Direction

With $pd$, however, the direction to be claimed is not known before the data, because it is the side the posterior favors. We therefore apply the penalty of the previous section to each direction in turn. With $\pi = .8$, for example, this gives two reweighted versions of the estimation prior, one that gives $\theta < 0$ probability $.8$ and so penalizes the claim $\theta > 0$, and one that gives $\theta > 0$ probability $.8$ and so penalizes the claim $\theta < 0$. The value $.8$ is treated as an upper bound, so every prior in between is also allowed, including the estimation prior with $.5$ on each side.

In general, the researcher fixes before the data an upper bound $\bar{\pi}$, between $.5$ and $1$. The class $\Gamma$, the set of priors considered, contains every prior obtained by reweighting the two halves of the estimation prior so that each side of $0$ has prior probability between $1 - \bar{\pi}$ and $\bar{\pi}$ (@fig-class shows the class for $\bar{\pi} = .7$ and $\bar{\pi} = .9$). With $\bar{\pi} = .5$, the estimation prior is the only prior in $\Gamma$, and no penalty is applied.

```{r}
#| label: fig-class
#| fig-cap: "The Class of Priors for Two Values of $\\bar{\\pi}$"
#| apa-note: >
#|   The priors in $\Gamma$ reweight the two halves of the estimation prior, here $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ (black), keeping the shape of each half; every prior in $\Gamma$, including the estimation prior, lies within the grey band. Panel A: for $\bar{\pi} = .7$, the prior probability of $\theta > 0$ lies between $.3$ and $.7$; the colored lines are the two extreme priors of the class, the one most skeptical of $\theta > 0$ (solid) and the one most skeptical of $\theta < 0$ (dashed). Panel B: the same for $\bar{\pi} = .9$, for which the prior probability of $\theta > 0$ lies between $.1$ and $.9$. A larger $\bar{\pi}$ gives a wider class.
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-pos: htbp
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

c_ex <- 0.975
w_a <- function(x, a) ifelse(x > 0, 2 * a, 2 * (1 - a))
ttl <- theme(legend.position = "top", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

# the estimation prior and the two extreme priors of the class, for a given pi0
lab3  <- c("mid", "low", "high")
labx  <- c("Estimation prior",
           expression("Most skeptical of " * theta > 0),
           expression("Most skeptical of " * theta < 0))
cols3 <- c(mid = "black", low = "#F8A31B", high = "deepskyblue3")
ltys3 <- c(mid = "solid", low = "solid", high = "dashed")
xa <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 2001); pa0 <- dnorm(xa)
class_plot <- function(p0, tag) {
  dA <- data.frame(theta = rep(xa, 3),
                   dens  = c(pa0, pa0 * w_a(xa, 1 - p0), pa0 * w_a(xa, p0)),
                   prior = factor(rep(lab3, each = length(xa)), levels = lab3))
  band <- data.frame(theta = xa, lo = pa0 * 2 * (1 - p0), hi = pa0 * 2 * p0)
  ggplot() +
    geom_ribbon(data = band, aes(theta, ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "grey85") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey40") +
    geom_line(data = dA, aes(theta, dens, colour = prior, linetype = prior), linewidth = 1.1) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = cols3, labels = labx) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = ltys3, labels = labx) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 2 * 0.9 * dnorm(0))) +
    labs(x = expression(theta), y = "Prior density", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL,
         title = bquote(bold(.(tag))*"   "*bar(pi) == .(sub("^0", "", format(p0))))) +
    theme_clean(15) + ttl
}
(class_plot(0.7, "A") | class_plot(0.9, "B")) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "top")
```

A claim about $\theta_i$ is made only if its posterior probability is at least $c$ under every prior in $\Gamma$. As in the previous section, these priors share the Bayes factor and differ only in the prior odds, so this probability is smallest under the prior that gives the claimed direction the lowest prior probability, $1 - \bar{\pi}$ (solid line in @fig-class for the claim $\theta > 0$). We call it the prior most skeptical of the claim. Under this prior, the posterior odds of the claim are those of the previous section with $\bar{\pi}$ in place of $\pi$, and the corresponding probability is
$$
pd_{\text{adj},i} = \frac{pd_i\,(1 - \bar{\pi})}{pd_i\,(1 - \bar{\pi}) + (1 - pd_i)\,\bar{\pi}}.
$$
A claim is made when $pd_{\text{adj},i} \geq c$, with the same threshold $c$ as before. Since $pd_{\text{adj},i}$ increases with $pd_i$, this requires $pd_i$ to reach the value
$$
c^* = \frac{c\,\bar{\pi}}{(1 - c)(1 - \bar{\pi}) + c\,\bar{\pi}}.
$$
With $c = .975$ and $\bar{\pi} = .8$, $c^* = `r nz(.975 * .8 / (.025 * .2 + .975 * .8), 4)`$. The adjustment is therefore equivalent to raising the threshold on $pd$ from $c$ to $c^*$. Since $\Gamma$ is fixed before the data, the data decide only which direction is claimed, and hence which prior in $\Gamma$ is the most skeptical.

Unlike $pd$, which is at least $.5$ by definition, $pd_{\text{adj}}$ can fall below $.5$. Take a parameter with $pd = .7$, favoring $\theta > 0$, and $\bar{\pi} = .8$. Its Bayes factor is $.7/.3 \approx 2.3$. Under the prior most skeptical of $\theta > 0$, the prior odds of $\theta > 0$ are $.25$ ($.2/.8$), so its posterior odds are $2.3 \times .25 \approx .58$ and $pd_{\text{adj}} \approx .37$. Under the prior most skeptical of $\theta < 0$, the prior odds of $\theta > 0$ are $4$ ($.8/.2$) instead, and its posterior probability is about $.90$. A value of $pd_{\text{adj}}$ below $.5$ does not mean that the data favor the opposite direction. It means that, with the skepticism allowed by $\bar{\pi}$, the data do not establish even which direction is more probable. In general, $pd_{\text{adj}}$ falls below $.5$ whenever $pd < \bar{\pi}$.

@fig-rule, Panel A, illustrates the rule for $\bar{\pi} = .7$, for which $c^* = .989$. Each bar spans the posterior probability of $\theta > 0$ across $\Gamma$, and its left end is $pd_{\text{adj}}$. A parameter with $pd = .980$ exceeds $c = .975$ under the estimation prior but not under every prior in $\Gamma$ ($pd_{\text{adj}} = `r nz(.98 * .3 / (.98 * .3 + .02 * .7), 3)`$), so no claim is made, whereas parameters with $pd = .990$ and $pd = .999$ are claimed. With $\bar{\pi} = .9$ (Panel B), the class is wider (@fig-class, Panel B), and $c^* = `r nz(.975 * .9 / (.025 * .1 + .975 * .9), 3)`$, so only the parameter with $pd = .999$ is claimed.

```{r}
#| label: fig-rule
#| dependson: fig-class
#| fig-cap: "The Resulting Rule for Two Values of $\\bar{\\pi}$"
#| apa-note: >
#|   For four parameters, the range of the posterior probability of $\theta > 0$ across $\Gamma$ (bars), whose left end is $pd_{\text{adj}}$, and its value under the estimation prior, $pd$ (circles). A claim is made only when the whole bar lies at or above $c = .975$ (dashed line), that is, when $pd_{\text{adj}} \geq c$, which is equivalent to $pd \geq c^*$. Panel A: for $\bar{\pi} = .7$, $c^* = .989$. Panel B: for $\bar{\pi} = .9$, $c^* = .997$. A larger $\bar{\pi}$ gives a wider class and longer bars, so fewer parameters are claimed; note the different scales of the x-axes.
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# range of Pr(theta > 0 | y) over the class, one bar per parameter, for a given pi0
post_a <- function(pd, a) pd * a / (pd * a + (1 - pd) * (1 - a))
pds <- c(0.97, 0.98, 0.99, 0.999)
rule_plot <- function(p0, tag, xmin, xby) {
  dB <- data.frame(eff = factor(sprintf("%.3f", pds), levels = sprintf("%.3f", rev(pds))),
                   lo = post_a(pds, 1 - p0), mid = pds, hi = post_a(pds, p0))
  dB$claim <- factor(ifelse(dB$lo >= c_ex, "claimed", "not claimed"), levels = c("claimed", "not claimed"))
  ggplot(dB, aes(y = eff)) +
    geom_segment(aes(x = lo, xend = hi, yend = eff, colour = claim), linewidth = 3.2, lineend = "round") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = c_ex, linetype = "dashed") +
    annotate("text", x = c_ex, y = 4.45, label = "italic(c) == '.975'", parse = TRUE, hjust = 1.08, size = 4) +
    geom_point(aes(x = mid), shape = 21, fill = "white", size = 3, stroke = 1.1) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("claimed" = "black", "not claimed" = "grey70"), name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(xmin, 1), breaks = seq(1, xmin, -xby)) +
    labs(x = expression(Pr(theta > 0 ~ "|" ~ italic(y)) ~ "across the class"),
         y = expression(italic(pd)),
         title = bquote(bold(.(tag))*"   "*bar(pi) == .(sub("^0", "", format(p0))))) +
    theme_clean(15) + ttl + theme(axis.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 1), axis.title.y = element_text(angle = 0, vjust = 0.5))
}
(rule_plot(0.7, "A", 0.925, 0.01) | rule_plot(0.9, "B", 0.75, 0.05)) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "top")
```

## What $\bar{\pi}$ Means and How to Choose It

The bound $\bar{\pi}$ says how skeptical the researcher is of a directional claim before the data. Under the prior in $\Gamma$ most skeptical of a claim, the claimed direction has prior probability $1 - \bar{\pi}$ and the opposite direction $\bar{\pi}$. With $\bar{\pi} = .5$ there is no penalty, and with $\bar{\pi} = .8$ a claim needs a Bayes factor four times larger than without the adjustment.

We use the same $\bar{\pi}$ for every parameter in a family. This requires the parameters to be exchangeable in direction, that is, the researcher has no reason to judge one parameter more likely than another to be positive, or more likely to be negative. Because the same bound then applies to every parameter, a prior probability can also be read as an expected proportion. A prior that gives the positive direction probability $.3$ for every parameter, for example, expects 30% of the parameters in the family to be positive. Under the priors in $\Gamma$, the expected proportion of parameters in each direction thus lies between $1 - \bar{\pi}$ and $\bar{\pi}$.

Through this proportion, null effects can guide the choice of $\bar{\pi}$. If up to 70% of the effects in a family could be null, at most 30% lie in each direction, so the class should allow each direction a prior probability as low as $.3$. The priors in $\Gamma$ give no probability to $0$, so the share of the null effects goes to the opposite direction, which gives $\bar{\pi} = .7$. This choice concerns both directions and is made before the data. The proportion of effects that could be null is thus a reference value for $\bar{\pi}$, and larger values give fewer false claims. Because the null effects enter only through this choice, the posterior probability $pd_{\text{adj}}$ remains a probability about the direction of a parameter, and $1 - c$ bounds the probability that a claim has the wrong direction.

A skeptical researcher can also use a narrow, informative estimation prior. Such a prior shrinks every estimate toward $0$, so fewer claims reach the threshold and the error rates are lower. The estimation prior, however, describes what is known about the size of each parameter, and this does not change when more parameters are tested. With the adjustment, the estimation prior stays as it is, and $\bar{\pi}$ checks whether each claim also holds under the other priors in $\Gamma$, without refitting the model and without changing the estimates.

For independent parameters, $\bar{\pi}$ can also be set through a fixed $\Pr(H_0)$, as in @Jeffreys1938 and @Westfall1997. Choosing $\bar{\pi}$ from the proportion of null effects keeps it the same whatever the size of the family, which suits the aim of keeping the proportion of false claims low. A fixed $\Pr(H_0)$ instead makes $\bar{\pi}$ grow with the size of the family, which suits the aim of avoiding any false claim.

# Simulation Study

## Design

The simulation design crossed four factors: the number of parameters in the family, $m$ (4, 8, 10, or 20); the proportion of null effects, $\pi_0$ ($.5, .6, \dots, 1$); the sample size, $n$ (30, 50, or 100); and the correlation between variables, $\rho$ ($0$ or $.8$). For each of the 144 conditions, we generated 10,000 data sets.

In each data set, the number of null effects was drawn from $\mathrm{Binomial}(m, \pi_0)$. Null effects had $\theta_i = 0$, and the other parameters had $\theta_i = 0.3$. The data set then consisted of $n$ observations of $m$ variables, drawn from a multivariate normal distribution with means $\theta_1, \dots, \theta_m$, unit variances, and the same correlation $\rho$ between every pair of variables. Each $\theta_i$ had an independent prior $\mathcal{N}(0, \tau)$, with $\tau = 2$. With the covariance matrix treated as known, the posterior of the $m$ parameters was multivariate normal, and each $pd_i$ was computed exactly from its marginal distribution. We applied the rule $pd_{\text{adj}} \geq c$, with $c = .975$, to every data set with $\bar{\pi} = .5, .6, \dots, .9$, where $\bar{\pi} = .5$ is the unadjusted rule, and with $\bar{\pi}$ set through a fixed $\Pr(H_0) = .5$, so that $\bar{\pi} = .5^{1/m}$ grows with the family size. We refer to the conditions with $\rho = 0$ and $\rho = .8$ as independent and correlated parameters, because the posteriors of the parameters are then independent or correlated.

For each data set, let $R$ be the total number of claims and $V$ the number of false claims. Claims regarding null effects were false regardless of direction, whereas claims regarding an effect of 0.3 were false only if they asserted $\theta_i < 0$. We evaluated the FDR, $\mathbb{E}[V/\max(R, 1)]$ [@Benjamini1995; @Benjamini2005]; the FWER, $\Pr(V > 0)$; and average power, the proportion of non-null effects claimed in the correct direction. Under this design, the probability of a wrong-sign claim was at most $.00015$, so nearly all false claims were claims about null effects. 


## Error Rates and Power of the Prior-Odds Rule

```{r}
#| label: sim-numbers
#| include: false
# numbers reported in the text of this section
mt <- df_pi0 |> filter(near(pi0, pi0_true))      # matched pi.bar
fdr_unadj_max  <- max(df_pi0$FDR[near(df_pi0$pi0, 0.5)])
fdr_mt_min     <- min(mt$FDR)
fdr_mt_max     <- max(mt$FDR)
fdr_under      <- df_pi0 |> filter(m == 20, n == 50, near(pi0, 0.6), near(pi0_true, 0.9)) |> pull(FDR)
pw_unadj       <- df_pi0 |> filter(m == 20, n == 50, near(pi0, 0.5)) |> pull(pw) |> mean(na.rm = TRUE)
pw_90          <- df_pi0 |> filter(m == 20, n == 50, near(pi0, 0.9)) |> pull(pw) |> mean(na.rm = TRUE)
# trade-off when pi.bar is one step below or above the matched value (m = 20, n = 50, pi0 = .8)
tr <- df_pi0 |> filter(m == 20, n == 50, near(pi0_true, 0.8)) |> mutate(pibar = sprintf("%.1f", pi0))
tr_fdr <- setNames(tr$FDR, tr$pibar)
tr_pw  <- setNames(tr$pw, tr$pibar)
fwer_mt4  <- max(mt$FWER[mt$m == 4])
fwer_mt20 <- max(mt$FWER[mt$m == 20])
fwer_unadj_max <- max(df_pi0$FWER[near(df_pi0$pi0, 0.5)])
fwer_90_max    <- max(df_pi0$FWER[near(df_pi0$pi0, 0.9)])
fwer_h0_max    <- max(df_h0$FWER)
```

The main aim of the prior-odds rule is to keep the proportion of false claims low, so the figures of this section show its FDR and power, and the Supplementary Material shows its FWER. In practice, the proportion of null effects is not known, so the researcher may set $\bar{\pi}$ too low or too high. We therefore applied every $\bar{\pi}$ to every $\pi_0$ (except $\bar{\pi} = 1$). In @fig-ind-fdr-pw and @fig-cor-fdr-pw, the outlined cells mark the matched value, $\bar{\pi} = \pi_0$, and the other cells of the same column show a $\bar{\pi}$ set too low (below) or too high (above). 

@fig-ind-fdr-pw Panel A shows the FDR for independent parameters. For the unadjusted rule (row $\bar{\pi} = .5$), the FDR grows with the family size and with $\pi_0$, and reaches $`r nz(fdr_unadj_max)`$ when $m = 20$ and all effects are null. With a matched $\bar{\pi}$, it lies between $`r nz(fdr_mt_min)`$ and $`r nz(fdr_mt_max)`$ across all conditions, with the largest values in the largest families and smallest samples. A $\bar{\pi}$ set too low raises the FDR, which becomes high when $\bar{\pi}$ is well below $\pi_0$ in a large family. With $m = 20$ and $n = 50$, for example, $\bar{\pi} = .6$ gives an FDR of $`r nz(fdr_under)`$ when $\pi_0 = .9$.

A lower FDR costs power (@fig-ind-fdr-pw, Panel B). Power depends on $\bar{\pi}$ and $n$, but not on $m$ or $\pi_0$, because $pd_{\text{adj}}$ depends only on the $pd$ of the parameter and on $\bar{\pi}$, not on the size of the family. Panel B therefore shows $m = 20$ only. With $n = 50$, for example, power falls from $`r nz(pw_unadj)`$ for the unadjusted rule to $`r nz(pw_90)`$ with $\bar{\pi} = .9$. The choice of $\bar{\pi}$ is thus a trade-off between false claims and power, and the matched value is a reference point within it. With $m = 20$, $n = 50$, and $\pi_0 = .8$, for example, the matched $\bar{\pi}$ gives an FDR of $`r nz(tr_fdr[["0.8"]])`$ and a power of $`r nz(tr_pw[["0.8"]])`$. Setting $\bar{\pi} = .7$ raises them to $`r nz(tr_fdr[["0.7"]])`$ and $`r nz(tr_pw[["0.7"]])`$, and setting $\bar{\pi} = .9$ lowers them to $`r nz(tr_fdr[["0.9"]])`$ and $`r nz(tr_pw[["0.9"]])`$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ind-fdr-pw
#| fig-cap: "False Discovery Rate and Power of the Prior-Odds Rule"
#| apa-note: >
#|   False Discovery Rate (FDR, Panel A) and average power (Panel B) as a function of the true proportion of null effects, $\pi_0$ (x-axis), and the bound $\bar{\pi}$ set by the researcher (y-axis), by family size $m$ (rows, Panel A) and sample size $n$ (columns), with independent parameters. Panel B shows $m = 20$ only, because power does not depend on $m$, and omits $\pi_0 = 1$, where power is undefined. The row $\bar{\pi} = .5$ is the unadjusted rule, where the prior odds are one and $pd_{\text{adj}} = pd$; outlined cells mark matched values, $\bar{\pi} = \pi_0$. Each cell is the empirical FDR or power over 10,000 replications.
#| fig-width: 21
#| fig-height: 24
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-align: left

d_fdr <- df_pi0 |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    facet_m = factor(paste0("m = ", m), levels = paste0("m = ", sort(unique(m)))),
    facet_n = factor(paste0("n = ", n), levels = paste0("n = ", sort(unique(n)))))
fdr_heat <- ggplot(d_fdr, aes(x = factor(pi0_true), y = factor(pi0), fill = FDR)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(FDR, 2)), size = 8, color = "black", fontface = "bold") +
  # matched values: pi0 = pi0_true
  geom_tile(data = dplyr::filter(d_fdr, abs(pi0 - pi0_true) < 1e-9), fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 1.9) +
  facet_grid(facet_m ~ facet_n) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours = c("green4", "#B8E186", "#FFFFBF", "#F4A582", "#B2182B"),
    values  = scales::rescale(c(0, 0.09, 0.15, 0.20, 0.7), from = c(0, 0.7)),
    limits  = c(0, 0.7), oob = scales::squish, na.value = "grey90",
    breaks  = c(0, 0.10, 0.20, 0.40, 0.7),
    labels  = scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.01), name = "FDR",
    guide   = guide_colorbar(barheight = unit(8, "cm"), barwidth = unit(1, "cm"),
                             title.position = "top", title.hjust = 0.5)) +
  labs(x = expression(italic(pi)[0]), y = expression(bar(italic(pi)))) +
  theme_clean(28) +
  theme(legend.position = "right", strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
        axis.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 1), axis.title.y = element_text(angle = 0, vjust = 0.5))

p_pw_heat <- df_pi0 |>
    filter(pi0_true != 1, m == 20) |>
    mutate(
      m = factor(m, levels = sort(unique(m))),
      facet_label_m = factor(paste0("m = ", m),
                             levels = paste0("m = ", sort(unique(m)))),
      n = factor(n, levels = sort(unique(n))),
      facet_label_n = factor(paste0("n = ", n),
                             levels = paste0("n = ", sort(unique(n))))) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = factor(pi0_true), y = factor(pi0),
               fill = pw)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
    geom_text(aes(label = round(pw, 2)),
              size = 8, color = "black", fontface = "bold") +
    geom_tile(data = function(d) dplyr::filter(d, abs(pi0 - pi0_true) < 1e-9), fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 1.9) +
    facet_grid(facet_label_m ~ facet_label_n) +
    scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours  = c("#B2182B", "#FFFFBF", "green4"),
    values   = scales::rescale(c(0, 0.5, 0.8), from = c(0, 0.8)),
    limits   = c(0, 0.8),
    oob      = scales::squish,
    na.value = "grey90"
  ) +
    labs(
  x = expression(italic(pi)[0]),
  y = expression(bar(italic(pi))),
  fill = "power"
)+theme_clean(28)+
    theme(legend.position = "right",
          strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
          axis.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 1), axis.title.y = element_text(angle = 0, vjust = 0.5))

(fdr_heat/p_pw_heat)+
  plot_layout(heights = c(4, 0.9))+
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = c('A', '1'))
```

A $\bar{\pi}$ chosen from the proportion of null effects suits the aim of keeping the proportion of false claims low. If the aim is instead to avoid any false claim, the relevant error rate is the FWER, shown in Figure S1 of the Supplementary Material for independent parameters. For a fixed $\bar{\pi}$, the FWER grows with the family size and changes little with the sample size. It reaches $`r nz(fwer_unadj_max)`$ for the unadjusted rule when $m = 20$ and all effects are null, and stays at or below $`r nz(fwer_90_max)`$ with $\bar{\pi} = .9$. With a matched $\bar{\pi}$, it is at most $`r nz(fwer_mt4)`$ when $m = 4$, but reaches $`r nz(fwer_mt20)`$ when $m = 20$. Setting $\bar{\pi}$ through a fixed $\Pr(H_0)$, which raises $\bar{\pi}$ with $m$, removes this growth. With $\Pr(H_0) = .5$ (top row of each panel of Figure S1), the FWER stays at or below $`r nz(fwer_h0_max)`$ for every family size and sample size.

```{r}
#| label: cor-numbers
#| include: false
# numbers reported for the correlated structures, prior-odds rule
mt_cor <- df_pi0_cor |> filter(near(pi0, pi0_true))
fdr_rng <- function(st) range(mt_cor$FDR[mt_cor$structure == st])
fwer_mt20_70 <- mt_cor |> filter(n == 50, m == 20, near(pi0_true, 0.7)) |>
  dplyr::select(structure, FWER) |> tibble::deframe()
fdr_eq_hi <- mt_cor |> filter(n == 50, m == 20, near(pi0_true, 0.5)) |>
  dplyr::select(structure, FDR) |> tibble::deframe()
# pi.bar set too low: pi.bar = .6 with pi0 = .9 (m = 20, n = 50)
fdr_low <- df_pi0_cor |> filter(n == 50, m == 20, near(pi0, 0.6), near(pi0_true, 0.9)) |>
  dplyr::select(structure, FDR) |> tibble::deframe()
```

@fig-cor-fdr-pw shows the FDR and power for correlated parameters (Figure S2 in the Supplementary Material shows the FWER). Power is nearly the same as with independent parameters, because $pd_{\text{adj}}$ depends only on the posterior of each parameter. The FWER is lower with correlated parameters in every condition, for example, with a matched $\bar{\pi}$, $m = 20$, $n = 50$, and $\pi_0 = .7$, the FWER is $`r nz(fwer_mt20_70[["equi"]])`$ with correlated parameters and $`r nz(fwer_mt20_70[["independent"]])`$ with independent ones. The FDR is lower in most conditions, also when $\bar{\pi}$ is set too low. With $m = 20$ and $n = 50$, for example, $\bar{\pi} = .6$ gives an FDR of $`r nz(fdr_low[["equi"]])`$ when $\pi_0 = .9$, against $`r nz(fdr_low[["independent"]])`$ with independent parameters. It is slightly higher with correlated parameters only in some large families with few null effects, for example $`r nz(fdr_eq_hi[["equi"]])`$ instead of $`r nz(fdr_eq_hi[["independent"]])`$ with a matched $\bar{\pi}$, $m = 20$, $n = 50$, and $\pi_0 = .5$. Across all sample sizes, the FDR with a matched $\bar{\pi}$ lies between $`r nz(fdr_rng("equi")[1])`$ and $`r nz(fdr_rng("equi")[2])`$ with correlated parameters and between $`r nz(fdr_rng("independent")[1])`$ and $`r nz(fdr_rng("independent")[2])`$ with independent ones.

```{r}

Panel B shows $m = 20$ only, because power changes little with $m$, and omits $\pi_0 = 1$, where power is undefined. The row $\bar{\pi} = .5$ is the unadjusted rule; outlined cells mark matched values, $\bar{\pi} = \pi_0$. Each cell is the empirical FDR or power over 10,000 replications.
#| fig-width: 21
#| fig-height: 24
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-align: left

# as the previous figure, with correlated parameters
d_fdr_cor <- df_pi0_cor |>
  dplyr::filter(structure == "equi") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    facet_m = factor(paste0("m = ", m), levels = paste0("m = ", sort(unique(m)))),
    facet_n = factor(paste0("n = ", n), levels = paste0("n = ", sort(unique(n)))))

fdr_heat_cor <- ggplot(d_fdr_cor, aes(x = factor(pi0_true), y = factor(pi0), fill = FDR)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(FDR, 2)), size = 8, color = "black", fontface = "bold") +
  geom_tile(data = dplyr::filter(d_fdr_cor, abs(pi0 - pi0_true) < 1e-9), fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 1.9) +
  facet_grid(facet_m ~ facet_n) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours = c("green4", "#B8E186", "#FFFFBF", "#F4A582", "#B2182B"),
    values  = scales::rescale(c(0, 0.09, 0.15, 0.20, 0.7), from = c(0, 0.7)),
    limits  = c(0, 0.7), oob = scales::squish, na.value = "grey90",
    breaks  = c(0, 0.10, 0.20, 0.40, 0.7),
    labels  = scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.01), name = "FDR",
    guide   = guide_colorbar(barheight = unit(8, "cm"), barwidth = unit(1, "cm"),
                             title.position = "top", title.hjust = 0.5)) +
  labs(x = expression(italic(pi)[0]), y = expression(bar(italic(pi)))) +
  theme_clean(28) +
  theme(legend.position = "right", strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
        axis.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 1), axis.title.y = element_text(angle = 0, vjust = 0.5))

pw_heat_cor <- d_fdr_cor |>
  dplyr::filter(pi0_true != 1, m == 20) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(pi0_true), y = factor(pi0), fill = pw)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(pw, 2)), size = 8, color = "black", fontface = "bold") +
  geom_tile(data = function(d) dplyr::filter(d, abs(pi0 - pi0_true) < 1e-9), fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 1.9) +
  facet_grid(facet_m ~ facet_n) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours  = c("#B2182B", "#FFFFBF", "green4"),
    values   = scales::rescale(c(0, 0.5, 0.8), from = c(0, 0.8)),
    limits   = c(0, 0.8), oob = scales::squish, na.value = "grey90") +
  labs(x = expression(italic(pi)[0]), y = expression(bar(italic(pi))), fill = "power") +
  theme_clean(28) +
  theme(legend.position = "right", strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
        axis.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 1), axis.title.y = element_text(angle = 0, vjust = 0.5))

(fdr_heat_cor / pw_heat_cor) +
  plot_layout(heights = c(4, 0.9)) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

## Comparison With Other Bayesian Methods

```{r}
#| label: compare-numbers
#| include: false
# numbers reported in the text of the comparison (n = 50)
load(file.path("script", "output", "df_compare.rda"))
df_compare_cor <- df_compare
df_compare <- filter(df_compare_cor, structure == "independent")
c50     <- df_compare |> filter(n == 50)
band    <- c50 |> filter(method == "simultaneous")
mt50    <- c50 |> filter(method == "prior-odds", near(pi0, pi0_true))
joint20 <- c50 |> filter(method == "joint", m == 20)
fdr_joint_50  <- joint20$FDR[near(joint20$pi0_true, 0.5)]
fdr_joint_90  <- joint20$FDR[near(joint20$pi0_true, 0.9)]
fdr_joint_100 <- joint20$FDR[near(joint20$pi0_true, 1)]
# power of each procedure: joint rule (range), prior-odds rule with matched
# pi.bar (mean over m, at pi0 = .5 and .9), band (mean over pi0, at m = 4 and 20)
pw_joint_rng <- range(c50$pw[c50$method == "joint"], na.rm = TRUE)
pw_po_50     <- mean(mt50$pw[near(mt50$pi0_true, 0.5)])
pw_po_90     <- mean(mt50$pw[near(mt50$pi0_true, 0.9)])
pw_band_4    <- mean(band$pw[band$m == 4], na.rm = TRUE)
pw_band_20   <- mean(band$pw[band$m == 20], na.rm = TRUE)
# correlated structures (n = 50)
band_cor  <- df_compare_cor |> filter(method == "simultaneous")
pw_band20 <- band_cor |> filter(m == 20) |> group_by(structure) |>
  summarise(pw = mean(pw, na.rm = TRUE)) |> tibble::deframe()
pw_po90   <- df_compare_cor |> filter(method == "prior-odds", m == 20, near(pi0, 0.9)) |>
  group_by(structure) |> summarise(pw = mean(pw, na.rm = TRUE)) |> tibble::deframe()
fwer_band_cor <- max(band_cor$FWER[band_cor$structure != "independent"])
fdr_joint_null20 <- df_compare_cor |> filter(method == "joint", m == 20, pi0_true == 1) |>
  dplyr::select(structure, FDR) |> tibble::deframe()
fdr_joint_half20 <- df_compare_cor |> filter(method == "joint", m == 20, near(pi0_true, 0.5)) |>
  dplyr::select(structure, FDR) |> tibble::deframe()
# power with m = 4 and pi0 = .9: prior-odds rule with matched pi.bar and band
pw_po_4_90   <- mt50$pw[mt50$m == 4 & near(mt50$pi0_true, 0.9)]
pw_band_4_90 <- band$pw[band$m == 4 & near(band$pi0_true, 0.9)]
```

We compare the prior-odds rule with two Bayesian alternatives. The first, hereafter the *joint directional rule*, orders the directional claims by their posterior probability and accepts the largest set whose joint posterior probability is at least $c$ [@Gelman2000; @Pruzek2016]. It claims the direction favored by the posterior, and what it limits is the posterior probability that any of the accepted claims has the wrong sign. The second, hereafter the *simultaneous-band rule*, computes credible intervals such that the joint posterior probability that every interval contains its parameter equals a set value, and claims a direction for a parameter whenever its interval excludes 0 [@Schnell2020; @Schnell2016; @Box1992].

The two procedures were applied to the same data sets as the prior-odds rule, for $n = 50$ and both values of $\rho$, using 10,000 draws from the joint posterior of each data set. All three procedures used $c = .975$. The joint directional rule requires a joint posterior probability of at least $.975$, the simultaneous band has a joint posterior probability of $.95$, and the prior-odds rule claims a direction when $pd_{\text{adj}} \geq .975$. @fig-compare shows their FDR, FWER, and power, together with those of the prior-odds rule with a matched $\bar{\pi}$ ($\bar{\pi} = \pi_0$).

With independent parameters, the simultaneous-band rule keeps both error rates low in every condition (its FWER ranges from $`r nz(min(band$FWER), 3)`$ to $`r nz(max(band$FWER), 3)`$). In contrast, the error rates of the joint directional rule increase with the proportion of null effects, and its FWER also with the family size. At $m = 20$, its FDR rises from $`r nz(fdr_joint_50)`$ at $\pi_0 = .5$ to $`r nz(fdr_joint_90)`$ at $\pi_0 = .9$ and $`r nz(fdr_joint_100)`$ when all effects are null. Lower Type I error comes with lower power. The power of the joint directional rule lies between $`r nz(pw_joint_rng[1])`$ and $`r nz(pw_joint_rng[2])`$ and decreases slightly with the family size. The power of the prior-odds rule with a matched $\bar{\pi}$ depends on $\pi_0$ rather than on $m$, and decreases from $`r nz(pw_po_50)`$ at $\pi_0 = .5$ to $`r nz(pw_po_90)`$ at $\pi_0 = .9$. The power of the simultaneous band depends on the family size rather than on $\pi_0$, and decreases from $`r nz(pw_band_4)`$ at $m = 4$ to $`r nz(pw_band_20)`$ at $m = 20$. The band thus has the lowest power in most conditions. The exception is small families with many null effects, where the matched $\bar{\pi}$ is large. With $m = 4$ and $\pi_0 = .9$, for example, the power of the prior-odds rule is $`r nz(pw_po_4_90)`$, against $`r nz(pw_band_4_90)`$ for the band.

```{r}
#| label: fig-compare
#| fig-cap: "False Discovery Rate, Family-Wise Error Rate, and Power of the Three Procedures"
#| apa-note: >
#|   False Discovery Rate (FDR, top row), Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER, middle row), and average power (bottom row) as a function of the true proportion of null effects, $\pi_0$ (x-axis), by family size $m$ (columns), with $n = 50$. Blue squares show the prior-odds rule with $\bar{\pi} = \pi_0$ (it stops at $\pi_0 = .9$ because with $\bar{\pi} = 1$ no claim would ever be made), orange circles the joint directional rule, and grey triangles the simultaneous-band rule. Line types and symbol fills show independent parameters ($\rho = 0$; solid lines, darker colors, filled symbols) and correlated parameters ($\rho = .8$; dashed lines, lighter colors, open symbols). The dotted horizontal line marks $.05$, and the grey band around it its 95% Monte Carlo band, that is, $.046$ to $.054$. Panel A shows all rates on their full scale; Panel B shows the two error rates between 0 and .12, where the band is visible.
#| fig-width: 21
#| fig-height: 24
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-align: left

lab_proc <- c(expression("Prior-odds, "*bar(italic(pi)) == italic(pi)[0]), "Joint directional", "Simultaneous band")
lab_cor  <- c("Independent", "Correlation .8")
d_cmp <- df_compare_cor |>
  # the prior-odds rule only with a matched pi0, which exists up to pi0_true = .9
  dplyr::filter(method != "prior-odds" | abs(pi0 - pi0_true) < 1e-9) |>
  dplyr::select(structure, method, m, pi0_true, FDR, FWER, power = pw) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(FDR, FWER, power), names_to = "metric", values_to = "rate") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    structure = factor(structure, levels = c("independent", "equi")),
    method  = factor(method, levels = c("prior-odds", "joint", "simultaneous")),
    metric  = factor(metric, levels = c("FDR", "FWER", "power"), labels = c("FDR", "FWER", "Power")),
    facet_m = factor(paste0("m = ", m), levels = paste0("m = ", sort(unique(m))))) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(rate))   # power is undefined when every effect is null
# reference line at .05 for the two error rates, with its 95% Monte Carlo band
# (10,000 replications; for the FDR, a mean of values in [0, 1], the band is conservative)
ref05 <- data.frame(metric = factor(c("FDR", "FWER"), levels = levels(d_cmp$metric)), y = 0.05)
mc_half <- qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(0.05 * 0.95 / 1e4)
ref05$lo <- 0.05 - mc_half; ref05$hi <- 0.05 + mc_half

# one color per procedure and structure: independent = darker with filled symbols,
# correlated = lighter with open symbols
cols  <- c("#1F4E9C", "#D98200", "grey25", "#4F8FDB", "#F5B335", "grey60")
fills <- c("#1F4E9C", "#D98200", "grey25", "white", "white", "white")
d_cmp$grp <- interaction(d_cmp$method, d_cmp$structure)   # prior-odds, joint, band; independent then .8

p_full <- ggplot(d_cmp, aes(x = pi0_true, y = rate, colour = grp, fill = grp, shape = method,
                  linetype = structure, group = grp)) +
  geom_rect(data = ref05, aes(xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = lo, ymax = hi), inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "grey85") +
  geom_hline(data = ref05, aes(yintercept = y), colour = "grey50", linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.6) +
  geom_point(size = 4.5, stroke = 1.8) +
  facet_grid(metric ~ facet_m, scales = "free_y", switch = "y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cols, guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = fills, guide = "none") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(22, 21, 24), labels = lab_proc, name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed"), labels = lab_cor, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0.5, 1, 0.1), labels = c(".5", ".6", ".7", ".8", ".9", "1")) +
  guides(shape = guide_legend(override.aes = list(colour = cols[1:3], fill = cols[1:3], linetype = "solid")),
         linetype = guide_legend(override.aes = list(colour = "grey20", fill = c("grey20", "white"), shape = 22))) +
  labs(x = expression(italic(pi)[0]), y = NULL) +
  theme_clean(28) +
  theme(strip.placement = "outside", strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical", legend.key.width = unit(2.5, "cm"),
        panel.spacing = unit(1, "cm"), axis.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 1))
# Panel A: all rates on their full scale; Panel B: the error rates near .05
p_zoom <- (p_full %+% dplyr::filter(d_cmp, metric != "Power")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.12)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.05, 0.10), labels = c("0", ".05", ".10"))
(p_full / p_zoom) +
  plot_layout(heights = c(3, 2), guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical", plot.tag = element_text(size = 34, face = "bold"))
```

With correlated parameters (dashed lines in @fig-compare), the results change mainly for the two procedures that use the joint posterior. The simultaneous band gains power. With $m = 20$, its power is $`r nz(pw_band20[["equi"]])`$ with correlated parameters and $`r nz(pw_band20[["independent"]])`$ with independent ones, while its FWER stays at or below $`r nz(fwer_band_cor, 3)`$. With correlated parameters and $m = 20$, the band thus has more power than the prior-odds rule with $\bar{\pi} = .9$ ($`r nz(pw_po90[["equi"]])`$). The FWER of the joint directional rule is lower than with independent parameters in every condition, and so is its FDR in most conditions. With $m = 20$ and all effects null, for example, its FDR is $`r nz(fdr_joint_null20[["equi"]])`$ with correlated parameters, against $`r nz(fdr_joint_null20[["independent"]])`$ with independent ones. Its FDR is higher only when few effects are null in families of ten or more parameters, for example $`r nz(fdr_joint_half20[["equi"]])`$ instead of $`r nz(fdr_joint_half20[["independent"]])`$ with $m = 20$ and $\pi_0 = .5$. The prior-odds rule keeps nearly the same power and has lower FWER, as described in the previous section.

The choice among the three procedures depends on the aim. If a small proportion of false claims is acceptable (FDR), the prior-odds rule is the most suitable, and in the simulations a $\bar{\pi}$ matched to the proportion of null effects kept its FDR between $`r nz(min(fdr_mt_min, fdr_rng("equi")[1]))`$ and $`r nz(max(fdr_mt_max, fdr_rng("equi")[2]))`$ in all conditions, with independent as well as correlated parameters. It is also the only one of the three procedures in which the researcher states, through $\bar{\pi}$, how skeptical they are of the claims before the data. If any false claim must be avoided (FWER), the simultaneous band is the more direct choice, because it kept the FWER close to or below $.05$ in every condition, although at the cost of power. The joint directional rule computes its probability under the estimation prior, so it keeps wrong claims rare when this prior describes how the parameters were generated [e.g., @Gelman2000]. This was not the case in the simulations, where many effects were exactly 0, and its error rates rose with the proportion of null effects. Its joint posterior probability is, however, useful when a set of claims and their directions are specified in advance and evaluated together as a single prediction (e.g., theory predicts $\theta_1 > 0$ and $\theta_2 > 0$).

The three procedures also differ in what they state about a set of claims. The joint directional rule and the simultaneous band are both computed from the joint posterior, so in a single step they give the claims and the probability that these claims hold together, up to the whole family of effects. The prior-odds rule instead reports a $pd_{\text{adj}}$ for each parameter, a researcher who also wants the probability that a set of claims, or the whole family, holds together has to compute it from the joint posterior.


# Application: Worked Example With the R Package `multibayes`

The procedures are implemented in the `multibayes` R package. The function `pd.adjust()` accepts either a matrix of posterior draws, from which $pd$ values are computed internally, or a vector of pre-computed $pd$ values. With draws, the null value of each parameter is set with the argument `null.value` (default 0), either as a single value for all parameters or as one value per parameter, for example a minimum effect of practical interest, with the estimation prior centered on it. The penalty is specified either directly as $\bar{\pi}$ (argument `pi.max`) or as $\Pr(H_0)$ (argument `p0`), from which $\bar{\pi} = \Pr(H_0)^{1/m}$. The threshold $c$, the posterior probability required to make a claim, is set with the argument `threshold` (default $.975$).

For this example, we use the openly available dataset from @Lin2020, who investigated the effect of ego depletion on conflict resolution across four studies. In their paradigm, an initial high-demand (vs. low-demand) task was followed by a Stroop task. For simplicity, we focus on Study 1, which tested the effects of congruency and ego depletion (within subjects). The dataset is readily accessible via the `afex` package [@Singmann2016] and was chosen for this reason; this example is not intended as a critique of the original work. Study 1 includes data from 253 participants, each completing 180 Stroop trials after each of the two tasks.

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE, tidy=FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("mar-cald/multibayes")
library(multibayes); library(brms); library(dplyr)

stroop1 <- subset(afex::stroop, subset = study == 1)
data_stroop <- stroop1 |>
  # remove useless levels id
  dplyr::mutate(id = droplevels(pno)) |>
  # select relevant variables
  dplyr::select(id, condition, congruency, trialnum, acc, rt) |>
  # previous trial within each block (participant x condition)
  arrange(id, condition, trialnum) |>
  group_by(id, condition) |>
  mutate(prev_cong = lag(congruency), prev_acc = lag(acc)) |>
  ungroup()
```

Given the repeated-measures structure of the data and the large number of trials per participant, we fit a multilevel generalized linear model using `brms` [@Paul2017] on reaction time (RT) data. A lognormal model was specified with the default flat priors, because they are the most common choice in applied work, not as a recommendation.

The model includes the effects of congruency (congruent vs. incongruent), previous congruency (congruent vs. incongruent), condition (depletion vs. control), and trial (position within the 180 trials of a condition, standardized). The sequential congruency effect was modeled as the interaction between congruency and previous congruency. A possible effect of depletion was modeled through condition and its interactions with congruency and trial, so that depletion could change response times overall, change the congruency effect, or change how either evolves over the trials.

The question of the study is whether ego depletion affects Stroop performance, so the family consists of the four effects involving condition (@tbl-hypotheses). The other effects, such as the congruency effect, are estimated but no claim is based on them, so they are not part of the family. For each of the four effects, the prior-odds rule says whether its direction can be claimed. The joint directional rule also gives the probability that the strongest claims, up to all four, hold together, and the simultaneous band gives intervals that contain all four parameters together with probability $.95$. 

| **Hypothesis** | **$\theta_\text{null}$** |
|----|:--:|
| $H_1$: condition effect | 0 |
| $H_2$: congruency $\times$ condition interaction | 0 |
| $H_3$: condition $\times$ trial interaction | 0 |
| $H_4$: congruency $\times$ condition $\times$ trial interaction | 0 |

: Tested Hypotheses for Reaction Times {#tbl-hypotheses}

We compute $pd$ as $\max\!\big(\Pr(\theta > 0 \mid y),\, \Pr(\theta < 0 \mid y)\big)$ for all hypotheses. When the direction of each parameter is specified in advance, the argument `direction` (`"greater"` or `"less"`, for each hypothesis) computes $pd$ as the posterior probability of the predicted direction, with the same threshold. The rule then corresponds to a single prior for each parameter, the member of $\Gamma$ most skeptical of the predicted direction, and $pd_{\text{adj}}$ is the posterior probability under that prior.


We retained only correct trials whose preceding trial in the same block was also answered correctly. This removed errors, trials without a response, the trials that followed either of them, and the first trial of each block, which has no preceding trial, yielding `r format(nrow(mod_rt$data), big.mark = ",")` observations.

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE, tidy=FALSE}
# correct trials preceded by a correct trial
data_rt <- data_stroop |>
  filter(acc == 1, prev_acc == 1)

# set contrast
contrasts(data_rt$congruency) <- contr.sum(2)/2
contrasts(data_rt$prev_cong) <- contr.sum(2)/2
contrasts(data_rt$condition) <- contr.sum(2)/2
# trial standardized (z-score)
data_rt$trial <- as.numeric(scale(data_rt$trialnum))

mod_rt <- brm(
  formula = rt ~ 1 + congruency * prev_cong +
    congruency * condition * trial +
    (1 + prev_cong + congruency * condition + trial * condition || id),
  family = lognormal(), data = data_rt,
  cores = 3, chains = 3, iter = 8000, seed = 1)
```

Since `pd.adjust()` computes $pd$ values automatically from a matrix of posterior draws, we extracted the draws of the four effects in the family and set $\bar{\pi} = .8$. Under the estimation prior, each direction of a parameter has prior probability $.5$; with $\bar{\pi} = .8$, we allow either direction of each parameter to have prior probability as high as $.8$, so a claim requires a Bayes factor four times larger than under the unadjusted rule. This is the reference value for a judgment that up to 80% of them could be null. It reflects skepticism about whether the depletion manipulation affects Stroop performance at all.

```{r, echo=TRUE}
draws_rt <- as.data.frame(mod_rt)
# the family: the four effects involving condition
par_names <- grep("^b_.*condition", colnames(draws_rt), value = TRUE)
draws_rt  <- draws_rt[, par_names]
pd.adjust(draws = draws_rt, pi.max = 0.8, null.value = 0)
```

```{r}
#| label: ex-counts
#| echo: false
ex   <- suppressWarnings(pd.adjust(draws = draws_rt, 
                                   pi.max = 0.8, null.value = 0))
EXc  <- attr(ex, "threshold"); EXcs <- attr(ex, "threshold.adj")
EXpd <- setNames(ex$pd, rownames(ex))
EXadj <- setNames(ex$pd.adj, rownames(ex))
EXn0 <- sum(EXpd >= EXc); EXn1 <- sum(EXpd >= EXcs)
num_word <- function(k) c("no", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine")[k + 1]
INT <- "b_congruency1:condition1"
# congruency effect (incongruent minus congruent, log RT) after each task;
# sum contrasts: congruent = +.5, control = +.5
fe <- brms::fixef(mod_rt)[, "Estimate"]
EXint_ctrl <- -(fe[["congruency1"]] + 0.5 * fe[["congruency1:condition1"]])
EXint_depl <- -(fe[["congruency1"]] - 0.5 * fe[["congruency1:condition1"]])
EXbelow <- names(EXadj)[EXadj < 0.5]
# joint directional statement and simultaneous band
EXj <- joint(draws_rt, interval = FALSE, null.value = 0)
EXb <- joint(draws_rt, interval = TRUE)
EXk <- sum(EXj$joint_cum >= 0.975)
band <- function(p, d) sprintf("[%.*f, %.*f]", d, EXb[p, "lower"], d, EXb[p, "upper"])
EXband <- rownames(EXb)[EXb$lower > 0 | EXb$upper < 0]
# the text below describes this pattern
stopifnot(EXn0 == 1, EXn1 == 1, EXpd[[INT]] >= EXcs, EXk == 1,
          identical(EXband, INT), fe[["congruency1:condition1"]] < 0,
          setequal(EXbelow, "b_condition1:trial"))
```

The printed header reports $m$, $\bar{\pi}$, the threshold $c$, and the value $c^*$ that $pd$ must reach. With the default $c = `r nz(EXc, 3)`$, a claim requires $pd_{\text{adj}} \geq `r nz(EXc, 3)`$, that is, $pd \geq `r nz(EXcs, 4)`$.

Only the congruency $\times$ condition interaction (`b_congruency1:condition1`) has $pd \geq c$, with $pd = `r nz(EXpd[[INT]], 4)`$, and it also has $pd_{\text{adj}} = `r nz(EXadj[[INT]], 3)`$, at or above $c$. The claim therefore holds under every prior in $\Gamma$. On the log scale, the congruency effect, the difference between incongruent and congruent trials, was `r nz(EXint_ctrl, 3)` after the low-demand task and `r nz(EXint_depl, 3)` after the high-demand task, so the claim is that the congruency effect is smaller after the high-demand task. None of the other three effects reaches $c$, with or without the adjustment. For one of them, the condition $\times$ trial interaction ($pd = `r nz(EXpd[["b_condition1:trial"]], 3)`$, $pd_{\text{adj}} = `r nz(EXadj[["b_condition1:trial"]], 3)`$), $pd_{\text{adj}}$ is below $.5$, so the priors in $\Gamma$ disagree on which direction is more probable, and the data do not establish even a leaning in either direction.

The function `plot()` draws, for each parameter, the range of the posterior probability of its favored direction across $\Gamma$ (@fig-example):

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
plot(pd.adjust(draws = draws_rt, pi.max = 0.8))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-example
#| fig-cap: "Posterior Probability of the Favored Direction Across the Class for the Four Effects Involving Condition"
#| apa-note: >
#|   Output of `plot()` for the worked example ($\bar{\pi} = .8$). Each bar spans the posterior probability of the favored direction across $\Gamma$, from $pd_{\text{adj}}$ (left end) to its value under the prior most favorable to that direction (right end); points mark $pd$, and the two ends of each range are printed on the right. ```
```

A companion function, `joint()`, implements the simultaneous-band rule and the joint directional rule compared in the simulation study. By default, it returns simultaneous equal-tailed credible intervals:

```{r, echo=TRUE}
joint(draws_rt, prob = .95)
```

Only the band of the congruency $\times$ condition interaction ($`r band(INT, 4)`$) excludes 0, so the simultaneous-band rule makes the same single claim.

Setting `interval = FALSE` returns instead the joint posterior probability of the $k$ strongest directional claims, for each $k$:

```{r, echo=TRUE}
joint(draws_rt, interval = FALSE, null.value = 0)
```

The rows are sorted by decreasing $pd$, and `joint_cum` gives this probability for the first $k$ rows. Here it is $`r nz(EXj$joint_cum[1], 4)`$ for the strongest claim alone and $`r nz(EXj$joint_cum[2], 2)`$ for the two strongest, so the joint directional rule at $.975$ also accepts only the claim about the congruency $\times$ condition interaction. In this family, the three procedures agree.

The last row gives the joint posterior probability for the whole family, that is, the probability that all four effects have the sign favored by their posterior, which is $`r nz(EXj$joint_cum[nrow(EXj)])`$. If the hypothesis of the study is read as depletion changing performance in all the ways the model allows, overall, in the congruency effect, and over trials, the data do not support it. The simultaneous band leads to the same conclusion, because the bands of the other three effects include 0. The data support only the narrower claim that depletion reduces the congruency effect.

# Discussion

The probability of direction ($pd$) is the posterior mass on the data-favored side of a reference point null value, equivalently, the larger of the two one-sided posterior probabilities. It is common practice to claim a direction whenever $pd$ exceeds a fixed threshold $c$, typically $.975$. Under an estimation prior symmetric about the null value, the direction selected after inspecting the data has the same prior probability as the opposite one, so each such data-selected hypothesis is evaluated at prior odds of one, and the rule $pd \geq c$ leaves these odds unchanged. With $m$ parameters that are independent a priori, the prior probability that every favored direction is wrong is then $.5^m$, so before the data it is almost certain that at least one of them is genuine. The procedure presented here builds on @Jeffreys1938 [see also @Westfall1997] and on Bayesian approaches to FDR control [@Scott2006; @Scott2010; @Guo2010; @Abraham2022; @Efron2001; @Storey2003; @Storey2002; @Stephens2017]. It requires each claim to hold even when its prior odds are lowered. The researcher sets how much they are lowered through a single quantity, $\bar{\pi}$, an upper bound on the prior probability of each direction of a parameter. A claim is then made when $pd_{\text{adj}}$, its posterior probability under the prior most skeptical of it, reaches the usual threshold $c$.

The derivation of the adjustment requires an estimation prior that is continuous and symmetric about the null value. The priors under which claims are evaluated are thus continuous and give point null effects no probability. Because the procedure evaluates only directional claims, not making a claim reflects the absence of a directional discovery, not evidence that the effect is null. Evaluating whether an effect is null requires other methods, such as those based on the spike-and-slab prior, which places probability exactly at the null value [@Scott2006; @Scott2010; @Stephens2017]. In Bayesian approaches to FDR control based on this prior, the proportion of null effects can be learned from the data [@Scott2010; @Stephens2017], but this requires large families [@Storey2002; @Efron2001], larger than those typical of psychological studies.

The proposed adjustment keeps the researcher's continuous prior, so every claim is a statement about the direction of a parameter, and null effects enter only through the choice of $\bar{\pi}$. A directional claim about a null effect is false, so when the parameters in the family are exchangeable in direction, $\bar{\pi}$ can be specified from a judgment about how many null effects the family could contain, instead of being learned from the data. In the simulations, a $\bar{\pi}$ matched to the proportion of null effects lowered the FDR relative to the unadjusted rule, with independent as well as correlated parameters. The FDR increased gradually when $\bar{\pi}$ was below the proportion of null effects and decreased, at the cost of power, when it was above it. A researcher may also choose a larger $\bar{\pi}$ deliberately, accepting this loss of power in exchange for fewer false claims. These results were obtained in the normal model, with independent or equally correlated parameters, and may differ in other settings.

Avoiding any wrong claim in the family is a different aim, for which a procedure built for the FWER is better suited. One such procedure is the simultaneous credible band [@Schnell2020; @Box1992], a set of intervals that contain all the parameters at once with posterior probability $.95$, in which a direction is claimed for each parameter whose interval excludes 0. In the simulations, the band had more power when the parameters were correlated. The joint directional rule instead accepts the claims with the largest $pd$, one after another, as long as their joint posterior probability stays at or above $.975$. This probability is computed under the prior used to fit the model, so it translates into few wrong claims only when the parameters follow this prior. In the simulations, the null effects were exactly 0, a value to which a continuous prior gives no probability, and the FDR and FWER of the rule grew with the proportion of null effects. Its FWER also grew with the size of the family. An advantage of both procedures is that they use the posterior of all parameters together, so they also give the probability that several claims hold together. With the prior-odds rule, which gives one $pd_{\text{adj}}$ per parameter, this probability requires a separate computation.

Applying the adjustment requires defining the hypothesis family to which it applies [@Hochberg1987; @Shaffer1995]. We favor the criteria proposed by @Westfall2011, where a family is a set of questions that *"form a natural and coherent unit, \[are\] considered simultaneously in the decision-making process, and/or present a set over which one plays pick-the-winner"*. Parameters on which no claim is based need not be included in the family. Whatever the definition, authors should clearly specify their family and explain how it serves the study's substantive goals.

We further recommend that researchers justify their choice of $\bar{\pi}$ by drawing on theory, expert elicitation, or domain expertise [@Hagan2019], and report this justification. Making this choice explicit serves two purposes. For researchers who use diffuse estimation priors, it states skepticism about the family without making the prior of any parameter narrower. For researchers who judge prior odds of one appropriate and decline the adjustment, it makes that commitment transparent.

A limitation is that applying the same $\bar{\pi}$ to every parameter assumes that they are exchangeable in direction. In many models this is not the case. A known main effect and an interaction term that motivated the study, for example, are typically not equally likely to be null. A common $\bar{\pi}$ set at the average proportion of null effects in the family is expected to keep the overall error rate close to that of an exchangeable family, because the rule applies the same threshold to every parameter. The errors, however, are distributed unevenly. The threshold is too strict for the more plausible claims, which lose power, and too lenient for the less plausible ones, among which false claims are more frequent. In such cases, the null value can differ across parameters. For the interaction term it can remain 0, whereas for the main effect, whose direction is known, it can be set to a minimal effect size of interest in that direction, with the estimation prior centered on it. Each claim then concerns whether a parameter lies above or below its own null value, so that the parameters can again be exchangeable in direction.

When the direction of an effect is not known, a minimal effect size of interest, $\delta$, can still be used, but the question changes from the direction of the effect to whether it lies outside the region $(-\delta, \delta)$ [@Kruschke2018]. A prior-odds penalty can be applied to this question as well, from the posterior draws and, in principle, without refitting the model, provided that the scale of the estimation prior is tied to $\delta$. Future work could extend `multibayes` in this direction and examine the error rates and power of this approach in families of tests.

As Bayesian methods become increasingly common in psychological research, often in pragmatic workflows with fixed decision thresholds, the implications of multiplicity should be explicitly recognized. Whatever the prior, a fixed threshold on the probability of direction leads to more wrong directional claims as the number of tests grows. The adjustment proposed here offers a simple step toward a more mindful use of such thresholds. The comparison with joint directional statements and simultaneous credible intervals, which the accompanying R package also implements, can help researchers choose the procedure that fits their aim.
